content_voiceover: The healthy endothelium is a busy antithrombotic factory with three functional groups worth memorizing. First, antiplatelet: nitric oxide and prostacyclin both inhibit platelet activation, while CD39 degrades ADP so platelets can't be recruited further. Second, anticoagulant: heparan sulfate on the endothelial surface potentiates antithrombin, thrombomodulin binds thrombin and flips its substrate specificity, so instead of cleaving fibrinogen, thrombin now activates protein C, and this reaction is boosted by the endothelial protein C receptor, or EPCR; tissue factor pathway inhibitor, TFPI, directly blocks the tissue factor-factor seven-a-factor ten-a complex. Third, profibrinolytic: tissue plasminogen activator and urokinase-type plasminogen activator convert plasminogen to plasmin to clear fibrin. The single highest-yield concept here is the thrombomodulin-protein C-EPCR axis, since defects in this pathway underlie activated protein C resistance and hypercoagulable states you'll see tested later in the thrombophilia section. Remember: injury or endothelial dysfunction flips this whole surface from antithrombotic to prothrombotic.
keypoints: TM + EPCR: thrombin activates Protein C instead of fibrinogen
keypoint_voiceover: Key groups to know: antiplatelet factors nitric oxide, prostacyclin, and CD39; anticoagulant factors heparan sulfate, thrombomodulin with EPCR activating protein C, and TFPI blocking the tissue factor complex; and profibrinolytic t-PA and u-PA. The thrombomodulin-protein C axis is the highest-yield piece to remember.
